evidence: Cic. Fin. 1.1: in variās reprehēnsiōnēs incurreret
Cic. Or. 1: verērī reprehēnsiōnem doctōrum atque prūdentium (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The commonest classical word for criticism, given or received: reprehēnsiōnem nōn fugere, not to escape criticism (Cic. Att. 10.3a.1); sine reprehēnsiōne, beyond criticism (Quint.). Properly a holding back (Cic. de Orat. 3.100).

terms.gloss: blame, censure; the opposite of praise
evidence: Cic. Att. 14.13.4: in vituperātiōnem cadere (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Blame as the opposite of laus; in rhetoric the speech of blame. Also blameworthy conduct (Cic. Verr. 2.5.101).

evidence: Cic. Q. Fr. 1.1.43: obtrectātiōne et malevolentiā līberātum
terms.comment: Criticism that comes from envy or ill will.

Classically the office of censor; as a judgement or criticism once in Ovid and then in post-Augustan prose (Vell., Plin., Gell.), and Lewis & Short thinks it probably not earlier than Augustus. Not for everyday fault-finding.

evidence: Suet. Aug. 4: Cassius Parmēnsis quādam epistulā sīc taxat Augustum (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Post-Augustan, says Lewis & Short; Traupman uses it for “tease” (Traupman 33), which it does not mean.

phrases.latin: Nōn eram nescius, Brūte, cum, quae summīs ingeniīs exquīsītāque doctrīnā philosophī Graecō sermōne tractāvissent, ea Latīnīs litterīs mandārēmus, fore ut hic noster labor in variās reprehēnsiōnēs incurreret.
phrases.english: I was well aware, Brutus, that when I set down in Latin what philosophers of the highest talent and the most refined learning had treated in Greek, this work of mine would run into criticism of every kind.
